prompt.context: Your client is Next Level Gaming (NLG), a start-up in the E-sports and computer gaming industry based in Los Angeles, California. NLG is planning to launch its first game -- an online, multiplayer role playing game that is unlike any existing franchise. Being a new player in the industry, NLG's CEO, Bobby Beck, has asked for your help in deciding its business model.
prompt.question: The company is considering 3 alternatives: (1) a subscription model where players pay a monthly fee; (2) a retail model where players pay full price at initial purchase; and (3) a free-to-play model where the game is free but charges players for in-game merchandise. How would you advise NLG to proceed?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for this decision?
clarifying_info.a: NLG is looking to launch immediately.
The online gaming industry is dominated by 3 major players who control 35%, 25%, and 20% market share respectively. There is a long tail of smaller gaming companies.
Based on preliminary market research, NLG expects the majority of players to be between the ages of 21 to 40.
NLG is planning to launch its game in the US only.

clarifying_info.q: What platforms will the game support?
clarifying_info.a: NLG's game is compatible for both Apple and Windows computers.

clarifying_info.q: What did it cost to develop the game?
clarifying_info.a: NLG spent $10 million USD to develop its first game.

exhibits.title: Revenue Assumptions by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table with three columns (Subscription, Retail, Free-To-Play) and rows for Target Audience, Predicted Market Share, % Buy In-Game Content, Monthly Subscription Fees, Retail Price, Annual In-Game Purchases, and a blank Predicted Revenues row for the candidate to calculate.
exhibits.data: Target Audience: 10M for all three models. Predicted Market Share: 10% Subscription, 12% Retail, 50% Free-To-Play. % Buy In-Game Content: 30% (Free-To-Play only). Monthly Subscription Fees: $10 (Subscription only). Retail Price: $60 (Retail only). Annual In-Game Purchases: $100 (Free-To-Play only).

exhibits.title: Cost Structure by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table with per-customer variable costs and fixed costs for each of the three models, plus a critical footnote about Free-To-Play cost applicability.
exhibits.data: Annual Variable Cost per customer: $50 Subscription, $22 Retail, $13 Free-To-Play. Customer Acquisition Cost: $35 Subscription, $18 Retail, $7 Free-To-Play. Fixed costs: Annual Product Dev $5M, Server Costs $7M, Other Fixed Costs $3M. Footnote: per-customer costs apply to all customers including non-paying; paying customers incur an additional average variable cost of $10.

exhibits.title: Beta Test Survey Results (n=100)
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart showing survey responses (scale 1-5, where 5 = most likely) for three business models (Subscription, Upfront Purchase, Free-to-Play) across four questions.
exhibits.data: Continue playing after year 1: Subscription 4.2, Upfront Purchase 1.2, Free-to-Play 4.1. Purchase add-ons to the base game: Subscription 4.0, Upfront Purchase 1.5, Free-to-Play 2.3. Recommend to friends: Subscription 1.2, Upfront Purchase 1.8, Free-to-Play 4.8. Switch to a new game in the same genre: Subscription 3.6, Upfront Purchase 4.2, Free-to-Play 1.9. Note: a higher value for the last question (Switch) is unfavorable.

framework: Break down profitability for each of the 3 models: (# players acquired) x ($ revenue per player) minus (fixed + variable costs)
Estimate the addressable market (US players aged 21-40) to anchor the total player pool
Calculate year-1 profit for each model using the provided revenue and cost assumptions
Assess qualitative factors: competitive response, customer acquisition and retention, alternate revenue streams
Consider future expansion potential: new platforms (mobile/console), new geographies, 2nd-generation games, e-sports tournaments

questions.prompt: Question 1 - Addressable Market Size: What factors would you consider to estimate the number of players NLG can target with its first game, and how large is this player base in the US?
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population by age (target 21-40), apply a PC ownership rate, then a gaming penetration rate. A reasonable chain: ~330M US population, ~28% aged 21-40, ~92M; ~70% PC ownership, ~64M; ~15% gaming propensity, ~10M. The casebook anchor is approximately 10 million players. Estimates significantly different from 10M should be pressure-tested.

math.setup: US population x share aged 21-40 x PC ownership rate x gaming penetration rate

questions.prompt: Question 2 - Profitability Calculations: What is NLG's expected first-year profitability under each of the 3 pricing models? (Show Exhibits 1 and 2)
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate revenues and costs for each model, then subtract for profit. Strong candidates also compute margins. The Exhibit 2 footnote is critical for Free-To-Play: the additional $10 variable cost applies only to the 30% paying customers, not all 50% who download. Subscription and Free-To-Play tie on absolute profit ($20M) but Subscription has the higher margin (16.7% vs 13.3%). The $10M R&D cost is sunk and should not factor into the decision.

math.setup: Revenue = market size x market share x price driver. Cost = (players x per-player variable costs) + fixed costs.
steps: Fixed costs total: $5M + $7M + $3M = $15M (same for all models)
Free-To-Play variable (all players): 10M x 50% x ($13 + $7) = 5M x $20 = $100M
Free-To-Play additional variable (paying only): 10M x 50% x 30% x $10 = $15M
math.answer: Subscription $20M profit (16.7% margin); Retail $9M profit (12.5% margin); Free-To-Play $20M profit (13.3% margin). Subscription and Free-To-Play tie on absolute profit; Retail is clearly inferior.

questions.prompt: Question 3 - Qualitative Brainstorm: What non-financial factors would you consider when comparing the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates structure brainstorming into MECE buckets. Key areas: (1) Competitive response -- how sticky is the player base if a rival launches a similar game? (2) Growth potential -- new platforms (mobile, console), new geographies, 2nd-generation games. (3) Alternate revenue streams -- merchandising, e-sports tournaments. (4) Consumer preference shifts -- migration to mobile, generational taste changes in game genres.

questions.prompt: Question 4 - Chart Interpretation: How does the survey data in Exhibit 3 impact your outlook on the 3 business models? Then give a final recommendation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should interpret all four survey questions. (1) Retention (continue playing after year 1): Subscription 4.2 and Free-to-Play 4.1 both high; Retail 1.2 very low. (2) Add-on purchases: Subscription 4.0 highest, Free-to-Play 2.3 moderate, Retail 1.5 low. (3) Referral (recommend to friends): Free-to-Play dramatically highest at 4.8; others low. (4) Churn risk (switch to new game) -- LOWER is better here; Free-to-Play 1.9 most loyal, Subscription 3.6 moderate risk, Retail 4.2 highest churn. Key insight: Retail shows low loyalty and low add-on potential. Free-to-Play benefits from viral growth and lowest churn. Candidate should note n=100 is statistically significant for directional insight. A higher value for the Switch question is unfavorable.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: How sticky is NLG's player base if a competitor launches a game in the same genre?
Free-to-play's large player base (50% share) creates higher network effects and switching costs vs. subscription (10%)
Subscription model offers more predictable defensibility through committed monthly payers

categories.name: Growth Potential
ideas: New platform expansion: PC to mobile or console
New geography: expansion outside the US
New game: launching a 2nd generation game to create fresh content
E-sports tournaments: viable once player base is sufficiently large

categories.name: Alternate Revenue Streams
ideas: E-sports tournament entry fees and sponsorships

categories.name: Consumer Preference Changes
ideas: Risk of players migrating to non-PC platforms (mobile, console)
Generational taste shifts may erode interest in the game genre over time
Trends in microtransaction acceptance vary by player demographic

recommendation: Recommend the free-to-play business model. It ties for the highest absolute profit ($20M) with subscription but captures a far larger player base (50% vs. 10% market share), creating a stronger competitive moat and viral growth engine (beta survey referral score: 4.8 vs. 1.2 for subscription).
The large installed base positions NLG well for future expansion into new platforms, geographies, and e-sports tournaments, and for launching a 2nd generation game with a ready audience.
The retail model is clearly inferior: lowest absolute profit ($9M), lowest margins (12.5%), and beta data shows very low retention (1.2) and highest churn risk (switch score: 4.2).
risks: Generating a sufficient share of paying players within the free-to-play base (modeled at 30% -- actual conversion could be lower)
Growing average revenue per paying player over time; in-game purchase fatigue is a real risk
Competitive entrants could undercut with a similar free-to-play model, eroding the 50% market share assumption
next_steps: Design two distinct in-game purchase value propositions: cosmetic upgrades (aesthetic appeal) and time-saving progression boosts, to sustain paying-player conversion across different player motivations
Conduct additional market research on the 21-40 age cohort's willingness to pay for in-game content to validate the 30% conversion assumption
Explore mobile and console platform expansion roadmap to diversify beyond PC and grow the addressable market
